title: Singleton Design Pattern
summary: Singleton constrains creation to exactly one safely-published instance. When duplication would corrupt state, why the standard implementations differ, and why to prefer injection instead.

refs.title: What is the Singleton Pattern? (Software Design Patterns) - YouTube

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: Singleton is not a sharing trick. It is a **creation constraint**: you make construction impossible for everyone except one controlled path, then you decide exactly when and how that path publishes the result. If you cannot state why a second instance would corrupt state or exhaust a resource, you do not need it.

A Singleton guarantees exactly **one live instance per scope** — usually per classloader in Java, per process in Python or Node — and provides a single, well-known access point to it. The mechanics are deliberately hostile to normal construction: the constructor is `private`, the instance lives in a `static` field, and the only way in is a static method like `getInstance()`. That method owns two jobs: decide **when** to create (eagerly at class load, or lazily on first call) and ensure **safe publication** so every thread sees a fully constructed object, not a half-initialised husk.

That definition exposes why experienced engineers distrust it. It fuses two unrelated responsibilities — **cardinality control** and **global visibility** — into one class. The first can be legitimate: a connection pool, a file writer, or a hardware driver physically cannot be duplicated without double-spending connections, interleaving bytes, or fighting over a device. The second is almost always a liability. Global visibility means any module can reach in, mutate shared state, and create invisible coupling across the codebase. You choose Singleton only when the cost of a second instance is correctness, not convenience. Shared access alone is never justification.

Every correct variant follows the same three moves, and the differences are only in timing and locking. First, **block the front door**: a private constructor means `new Config()` fails at compile time, so reflection and serialization become the only smuggling routes — both of which you must explicitly close. Second, **hold the reference statically**: a `private static` field is the single source of truth for identity. Third, **gate creation through one method**: `getInstance()` checks, creates once, and returns the same reference forever. Lazy versions add a concurrency protocol around the check-then-act; eager versions lean on the classloader, which already initialises statics exactly once and with a memory barrier. The WHY is publication: without a `volatile` write, a `synchronized` block, or class-initialisation semantics, Thread B can observe a non-null pointer to memory Thread A has not finished filling in.

blocks.title: Lazy Singleton access path
blocks.caption: Double-checked path: fast unsynchronised read, slow synchronised creation.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Caller calls getInstance] --> B{instance == null?}
  B -- No --> C[Return existing instance]
  B -- Yes --> D[Acquire lock]
  D --> E{Still null inside lock?}
  E -- No --> C
  E -- Yes --> F[Create via private constructor]
  F --> G[Publish via volatile write]
  G --> C

items: **Private constructor** — makes uncontrolled creation a compile error. Add a guard inside it that throws if an instance already exists, to defeat reflection.
**Static holder** — `private static volatile Instance` or a nested holder class. This field *is* the Singleton. Its declaration determines thread safety.
**Static accessor** — the only legal entry point. Contains the null check, the lock, and the return. Keep it narrow; never put business logic here.
**Safe publication** — `volatile`, `synchronized`, enum semantics, or class initialisation. Without one of these you have a race, not a pattern.

blocks.text: The implementation spectrum you must be able to write cold

Interviewers do not care that you memorised one version. They care that you can explain why the naive version breaks under threads and what each fix costs. `synchronized getInstance()` is correct and brutally slow on the hot path if you synchronise every call — though modern JVMs make uncontended locks cheaper than folklore suggests, it still serialises readers for no reason. Double-checked locking fixes the throughput problem by checking outside the lock and re-checking inside, but it is **broken unless the field is `volatile`**. Before Java 5 it was broken even with `volatile`; since the revised memory model, `volatile` forbids reordering of the constructor writes past the pointer publish, which is the entire bug. Bill Pugh's holder idiom and `enum` sidestep the protocol by letting the classloader do the locking once, at load time.

WHY the holder and `enum` win in Java interviews: they move concurrency from code you write to guarantees the platform already provides. No `volatile` to forget, no lock ordering to reason about, no fast-path versus slow-path benchmark to argue. The trade-off is control: eager initialisation pays construction cost at class-load time whether or not you ever use the object, and `enum` cannot lazily defer or take construction arguments. If you need lazy plus parameters — `init(url)` called once — you no longer have a pure Singleton; you have a one-shot registry, and you should say so explicitly and guard re-initialisation with an `AtomicReference.compareAndSet` or fail loudly on second `init`.

blocks.text: How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Singleton failures never look like pattern failures. They look like flaky reads, duplicated side effects, or tests that pass alone and fail together. The mechanism is always the same: either publication was unsafe, scope was misunderstood, or mutable state leaked through the global handle. In a large service the most expensive failure is not a crash — it is two objects both believing they are *the* instance, each holding a different view of the world.

blocks.title: The volatile line is load-bearing
blocks.text: If you write double-checked locking in Java and omit `volatile`, you have not written a Singleton — you have written a **race with a cache**. The JVM may publish the pointer before the constructor's writes complete. It will pass every unit test and fail at 3am under GC pressure. When the interviewer asks *why volatile*, the answer is **ordering, not visibility**: it bars store-store reordering across the publish.
Singleton versus just passing it in

Modern codebases rarely need the pattern because module scope plus dependency injection covers both halves better. A module-level object in Python or JavaScript already gives you single identity without a class ceremony, and a DI container can scope any bean as a singleton while keeping it an ordinary, constructor-injected parameter. The difference is **explicitness**: injected dependencies appear in signatures, can be replaced with fakes, and have a managed lifecycle with startup and shutdown hooks. A static `getInstance()` hides all three. Choose global access only for truly ambient, stable, unmocked infrastructure — a clock, an ID generator — and even then prefer injecting a `Clock` interface so tests can freeze time.

blocks.caption: Use it when duplication breaks correctness. Otherwise inject.
rows: Exactly one coordinator must exist: pool, sequencer, device driver, single writer
You just want convenient access — use a parameter, a context object, or DI scope
Construction is expensive and stateless reuse is provably safe
State varies per request, tenant, or test — you need a factory or scoped instance
Identity must be stable across unrelated call sites with no wiring path
Call graph allows explicit passing — hidden globals make reasoning harder for zero gain
Platform gives you safety for free: Java enum, holder idiom
Language makes statics per-module or per-isolate — you will get one-per-worker confusion

blocks.text: How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Write getInstance() thread-safe
items.text: Start with the holder idiom, not DCL. State why: class-initialisation lock is correct by construction. Only write DCL if asked for lazy with arguments, and narrate the `volatile` ordering argument as you write it.

items.title: Break your own code
items.text: Volunteer the three breakouts before they ask: reflection via private constructor, serialization without `readResolve`, and cloneable. Add the `INSTANCE != null` guard, `readResolve()`, and `final` class. Interviewers score this higher than the happy path.

items.title: Defend or kill the global
items.text: Expect: why not a static utility class? Why not DI? Answer crisply: static utilities carry no identity or lazy lifecycle; DI singleton scope is preferable in app code. Use raw Singleton only at library boundaries or where no container exists.

items.title: Scale the scope
items.text: Follow-up is always scope: what happens with two classloaders, two pods, or two threads calling `init(config)`? Correct answer: Singleton is per-classloader, not per-cluster. Distributed uniqueness needs a coordinator — database constraint, ZooKeeper lock, single-writer service — not a pattern.

items.title: Test it
items.text: Close by describing how you would test consumers: inject the interface, substitute a fake, reset state between tests. If state cannot be reset, the design is untestable and you should say you would replace the static access with injection.

items: **Singleton guarantees one instance globally** — false. It guarantees one per classloader or isolate. Two classloaders, two workers, or two containers each get their own *the* instance.
**`synchronized` on the method is the safe default** — correct but crude. It serialises every read. DCL with `volatile` or the holder idiom preserves safety without the hot-path lock.
**Enum is overkill** — backwards. In Java, a single-element `enum` is the shortest correct answer: reflection-proof, serialization-proof, and obviously intentional.

**Singleton and static class are interchangeable** — no. A static utility holds no identity, cannot implement an interface polymorphically, and cannot be lazily created or replaced. Singleton holds stateful identity.

**Making it a Singleton makes it thread-safe** — dangerous. Uniqueness says nothing about concurrent mutation. A Singleton wrapping a `HashMap` with setters is a shared race condition with a fancy name. Guard state with immutability or concurrent structures.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Singleton restricts a class to one safely-published instance reached through a single accessor — use the holder idiom or enum, guard reflection and serialization, and prefer DI scoping unless a second instance would corrupt correctness.**
